tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly.     name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }

    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }

# MPTokenAuthorize Transaction Overview

## Fields

The transaction includes two key fields beyond common transaction fields:

1. **MPTokenIssuanceID** (String/UInt192, Required): "The ID of the MPT to authorize."

2. **Holder** (Address/AccountID, Optional): "The holder to authorize. Only used for authorization/allow-listing; must be omitted if submitted by the holder."

## Flags

**tfMPTUnauthorize** (0x00000001, Decimal 1): Enables revocation of MPT holding when the holder has a zero balance, deleting their MPToken entry. Transactions fail if balance is non-zero or the token is locked.

## Authorization Mechanics

The documentation describes three distinct use cases:

1. **Holder Opt-in**: An account signals willingness to hold an MPT, creating a new MPToken entry with zero balance—required before receiving that MPT type in payment.

2. **Holder Revocation**: An account removes their willingness to hold an MPT by deleting their MPToken entry (zero balance, unlocked tokens only).

3. **Issuer Allow-listing**: "For an MPT that uses allow-listing, an issuer grants or revokes permission for another account to hold the given MPT."

The document does not explicitly detail the tfMPTRequireAuth flag behavior or distinguish issuer pre-authorization workflows separately from these three mechanisms.

# MPTokenIssuance Ledger Object

## Key Fields

**OutstandingAmount**: "The total amount of MPTs of this issuance currently in circulation. This value increases when the issuer sends MPTs to a non-issuer, and decreases whenever the issuer receives MPTs."

**MaximumAmount**: An optional field representing the upper limit of tokens that can exist simultaneously. If unspecified, the cap defaults to 2^63 - 1.

## Computing the MPTokenIssuanceID

The identifier is derived through a two-step process:

1. **Hash Computation**: Apply SHA-512Half to concatenated values:
   - MPTokenIssuance space key (0x007E)
   - Transaction sequence number
   - Issuer's AccountID

2. **ID Format**: The resulting 192-bit integer combines:
   - Transaction sequence number
   - Issuer's AccountID (concatenated in that order)

This construction ensures each issuance can be uniquely identified and distinguished from subsequent MPT creations by the same issuer account.

# MPT Payment Amount Structure

When sending Multi-Purpose Tokens, the `Amount` field uses a specialized format distinct from standard currency amounts.

## Field Structure

Instead of the typical `currency`, `value`, and `issuer` object, MPT payments require:

- **`mpt_issuance_id`**: A unique identifier for the specific MPT
- **`value`**: The numeric amount being transferred

As the documentation notes: "When you send a payment using MPTs, the _Amount_ field requires only the `mpt_issuance_id` and the `value`."

## Example JSON

```json
{
  "Account": "rLWSJKbwYSzG32JuGissYd66MFTvfMk4Bt",
  "Amount": {
    "mpt_issuance_id": "006419063CEBEB49FC20032206CE0F203138BFC59F1AC578",
    "value": "100"
  },
  "Destination": "raZ3wTTKiMHn3BiStvz4ET9rbCHfU1DMak",
  "TransactionType": "Payment"
}
```

## Key Limitation

"Version 1 MPTokens only support direct MPT payment between accounts. They cannot be traded in the decentralized exchange," restricting their use to peer-to-peer transfers without DEX integration.

# MPToken Ledger Entry Fields

## Core Balance Field

**MPTAmount** is the primary field tracking holder balances. It stores "The amount of tokens currently held by the owner" with a range from 0 to 2^63-1.

## Key Authorization Flag

**lsfMPTAuthorized** (value 0x00000002) indicates issuer approval status. The documentation notes this flag shows the issuer has "authorized the holder for the MPT" in allow-listing scenarios, and can be toggled via MPTokenAuthorize transactions.

## Additional Relevant Fields

- **Account**: Identifies the token holder's address
- **MPTokenIssuanceID**: References the specific token issuance
- **LockedAmount**: Tracks tokens in escrow (when TokenEscrow amendment is active)
- **lsfMPTLocked** (0x00000001): Companion flag indicating tokens are locked and restricted from most transactions

The MPToken entry essentially functions as a holder's account statement for a specific multi-purpose token issuance, with authorization status managed through transaction flags.

# MPTokenIssuanceCreate Transaction Reference

## Overview
The MPTokenIssuanceCreate transaction establishes a new Multi-purpose Token (MPT) issuance, defining token properties. The sender becomes the MPT's issuer. This requires the MPTokensV1 amendment.

## Required Fields
- **TransactionType**: "MPTokenIssuanceCreate"
- **Account**: Issuer's address

## Optional Fields

| Field | Type | Description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| AssetScale | Number (0-255) | Decimal places for display; default is 0 |
| TransferFee | Number (0-50,000) | Secondary sale fee in basis points |
| MaximumAmount | String | "Maximum asset amount that can be issued; default is 2^63-1" |
| MPTokenMetadata | Hex String | "Arbitrary metadata about issuance; limit 1024 bytes" |
| DomainID | Hash | Permissioned domain ledger entry ID (requires PermissionedDomains + SingleAssetVault amendments) |
| ImmutableFlags | Number | Flags declaring immutable fields (requires DynamicMPT amendment) |

## Transaction Flags

| Flag Name | Hex | Decimal | Purpose |
|-----------|-----|---------|---------|
| tfMPTCanLock | 0x02 | 2 | Enable global/individual locking |
| tfMPTRequireAuth | 0x04 | 4 | Require holder authorization |
| tfMPTCanEscrow | 0x08 | 8 | Allow escrow placement |
| tfMPTCanTrade | 0x10 | 16 | Enable DEX trading |
| tfMPTCanTransfer | 0x20 | 32 | Allow transfers between non-issuers |
| tfMPTCanClawback | 0x40 | 64 | Enable issuer clawback capability |
| tfMPTCanHoldConfidentialBalance | 0x80 | 128 | Support confidential transfers (ConfidentialTransfer amendment) |

## Immutable Flags (DynamicMPT amendment)
Parallel flags (tif-prefixed) lock corresponding properties permanently: tifMPTCanLock, tifMPTRequireAuth, tifMPTCanEscrow, tifMPTCanTrade, tifMPTCanTransfer, tifMPTCanClawback, tifMPTCanHoldConfidentialBalance, tifMPTMetadata (65536), tifMPTTransferFee (131072).

## Example JSON
```json
{
  "TransactionType": "MPTokenIssuanceCreate",
  "Account": "rNFta7UKwcoiCpxEYbhH2v92numE3cceB6",
  "AssetScale": 4,
  "TransferFee": 0,
  "MaximumAmount": "50000000",
  "MPTokenMetadata": "7B2274223A225442494C4C222C...",
  "Fee": "12",
  "Flags": 122,
  "Sequence": 99536574
}
```

## Key Error Conditions
- **temMALFORMED**: Non-zero transfer fee without tfMPTCanTransfer flag
- **temDISABLED**: Required amendment not enabled
- **tecINSUFFICIENT_RESERVE**: Insufficient XRP for reserve requirement
- **tecDIR_FULL**: Owner directory at capacity

# xrpl.js Changelog: MPT Support History

## Version 5.3.0 (2026-09-16)
**Added:** Support for `LendingProtocolV1_1`.

## Version 5.2.0 (2026-09-11)
**Changed:** The library now supports `fixCleanup3_4_0` signing prefixes.

## Version 5.1.0 (2026-08-24)
**Added:** This release introduced comprehensive sponsorship capabilities and expanded MPT functionality. Notable additions include "Support Dynamic MPTs (XLS-94d) based on latest spec change" and "Add `ReferenceHolding` to `MPTokenIssuance` ledger object and `vault_info` response." The version also included "Support for Confidential Transfers for Multi-Purpose Tokens (XLS-0096)."

## Version 5.0.0 (2026-06-05)
**Key Changes:** ED25519 became the default signing algorithm, and the library addressed network ID validation more strictly. The release notes indicate improved handling of `NetworkID` field inclusion in transactions.

## Version 4.4.3 (2025-11-07)
**Added:** The release exported `Batch` (XLS-56) transaction types. It also introduced utility functions: "Add `encodeMPTokenMetadata` and `decodeMPTokenMetadata` helper functions to encode and decode MPTokenMetadata as per XLS-89 standard."

import {
  BaseTransaction,
  isString,
  validateBaseTransaction,
  validateRequiredField,
  Account,
  validateOptionalField,
  isAccount,
  GlobalFlagsInterface,
} from './common'

/**
 * Transaction Flags for an MPTokenAuthorize Transaction.
 *
 * @category Transaction Flags
 */
export enum MPTokenAuthorizeFlags {
  /**
   * If set and transaction is submitted by a holder, it indicates that the holder no
   * longer wants to hold the MPToken, which will be deleted as a result. If the the holder's
   * MPToken has non-zero balance while trying to set this flag, the transaction will fail. On
   * the other hand, if set and transaction is submitted by an issuer, it would mean that the
   * issuer wants to unauthorize the holder (only applicable for allow-listing),
   * which would unset the lsfMPTAuthorized flag on the MPToken.
   */
  tfMPTUnauthorize = 0x00000001,
}

/**
 * Map of flags to boolean values representing {@link MPTokenAuthorize} transaction
 * flags.
 *
 * @category Transaction Flags
 */
export interface MPTokenAuthorizeFlagsInterface extends GlobalFlagsInterface {
  tfMPTUnauthorize?: boolean
}

/**
 * The MPTokenAuthorize transaction is used to globally lock/unlock a MPTokenIssuance,
 * or lock/unlock an individual's MPToken.
 */
export interface MPTokenAuthorize extends BaseTransaction {
  TransactionType: 'MPTokenAuthorize'
  /**
   * Identifies the MPTokenIssuance
   */
  MPTokenIssuanceID: string
  /**
   * An optional XRPL Address of an individual token holder balance to lock/unlock.
   * If omitted, this transaction will apply to all any accounts holding MPTs.
   */
  Holder?: Account
  Flags?: number | MPTokenAuthorizeFlagsInterface
}

/**
 * Verify the form and type of an MPTokenAuthorize at runtime.
 *
 * @param tx - An MPTokenAuthorize Transaction.
 * @throws When the MPTokenAuthorize is Malformed.
 */
export function validateMPTokenAuthorize(tx: Record<string, unknown>): void {
  validateBaseTransaction(tx)
  validateRequiredField(tx, 'MPTokenIssuanceID', isString)
  validateOptionalField(tx, 'Holder', isAccount)
}

## MPTokenAuthorize Overview

The MPTokenAuthorize transaction is submitted by a holder to create an MPToken ledger entry on their account.

## Key Roles: Holder, Issuer, and Require Auth

The authorization process is performed by both the Holder and the Issuer if Require Auth is enabled. 

When the Require Auth flag is enabled, holders must get explicit approval from the issuer before they can hold the token—in other words, it uses allow-listing. If the issuance enables allow-listing, the opt-in is two-sided: the holder authorizes the MPT first, and then you authorize the holder with your own MPTokenAuthorize transaction.

## Authorization Order

Any account that wants to hold an MPT, whether sending or receiving, must opt in first.

## Sending MPTs

Holders can send the MPT to each other only if the issuance has the Can Transfer flag enabled, and both parties are authorized.

29	  const { meta } = response.result
30	  if (meta == null || typeof meta === 'string') {
31	    throw new Error(`${label}: transaction metadata unavailable`)
32	  }
33	  if (meta.TransactionResult !== 'tesSUCCESS') {
34	    throw new Error(`${label} failed: ${meta.TransactionResult}`)

62	    ledger_index: 'validated',
63	  })
64	  const node = response.result.node as unknown as LedgerEntry.MPToken
65	  if (node.LedgerEntryType !== 'MPToken') {

## Summary

**Research done first:**
- `xrpl` npm latest is **5.3.0** — MPT support (XLS-33) landed in 4.1.0 and matured through 4.4.0/5.1.0 with metadata helpers and Dynamic MPT support.
- Read the xrpl.org docs for `MPTokenIssuanceCreate`, `MPTokenAuthorize`, `Payment` (MPT amount format), and the `MPTokenIssuance`/`MPToken` ledger objects; confirmed via the actual `.ts` source shipped in the installed package that field names/casing matched (`MPTokenIssuanceID`, `mpt_issuance_id`, `MPTAmount`, `OutstandingAmount`, etc.).
- Queried the testnet server directly (`feature` RPC on `s.altnet.rippletest.net:51234`) and confirmed **`MPTokensV1` is enabled** (so MPTs work) and `DynamicMPT` is disabled (so I avoided `ImmutableFlags`).
- Used latest TypeScript (7.0.2) and `@types/node` (26.6.3). Note: `ts-node` doesn't yet support TS7's restructured internals, so I dropped it and run via plain `tsc` + `node` instead — simpler and doesn't need a workaround.

**Project** (`/private/tmp/ws/a07342828b53/project`): strict-mode TypeScript project (`src/index.ts`) that:
1. Issues an MPT from your account with `tfMPTRequireAuth` (allow-listing only).
2. Funds a fresh testnet holder account via the faucet, has it opt in, then issuer-approves it via `MPTokenAuthorize`.
3. Sends 1,000 units via a `Payment` with an MPT amount.
4. Reads the holder's balance and outstanding supply back via `ledger_entry` (`mptoken` / `mpt_issuance`).
